title: What is wealth management?
subtitle: Net worth, asset allocation and the portfolio you should expect
openingQuestion: What does wealth management actually manage first?
explanation: Wealth management is broader than portfolio management: it starts from the personal balance sheet, from goals with specific dates attached, from cash coming in and going out, and from the capacity to absorb volatility. Investing is only one part of it, and usually not the decisive part. The two areas most often skipped but far more consequential are liquidity for short-term needs and protection against large risks - because one unhedged accident can erase years of accumulation.

realWorldExample.description: A good wealth management plan does not only maximise return; it also makes sure the money is there for education, a home, retirement, and protection against risk.

quiz.question: Where does wealth management start?
options: The return target you would like to hit each year
The list of stocks and funds currently recommended
The minimum capital needed to start investing at all
Net worth, goals, cash flow and risk appetite together
quiz.explanation: Investing is only one part of the picture. Choosing products before you know what you own, when you will need the money and how much volatility you can live with is doing the sequence backwards - the portfolio then serves itself rather than any goal. A return target with no horizon attached is a wish, a recommendation list is a product menu, and a minimum capital figure is a sales threshold, not a plan.

quiz.question: Why does asset allocation matter more than picking the right single stock?
options: Because the weights between asset classes drive most of the variation
Because trading costs on individual names are far higher than on funds
Because names within one asset class always move in exactly the same way
Because picking the right name is something nobody can actually do
quiz.explanation: The split between equities, bonds and cash determines most of a portfolio's swing. One big winner inside a small slice of the portfolio rarely offsets an allocation that is out of line with your risk appetite and your time horizon. Trading costs are real but second order, names inside a class are correlated rather than identical, and skilled selection is difficult rather than impossible.

quiz.question: Which asset usually sits in the most liquid group?
options: Unlisted growth company shares
Cash and bank deposits
Long-term rental property
Collectibles and precious metals
quiz.explanation: Liquidity is the first thing to settle when building a personal balance sheet, because it decides what you can reach without selling something at a bad price. Cash and deposits convert at face value on demand. Unlisted shares may take months to sell and often at a discount, rental property takes months at best, and collectibles depend entirely on finding a particular buyer.

quiz.question: A family needs to use a house-purchase fund in 3 years. Which priority is right?
options: Favour equities, 3 years counts as long term
Favour the highest liquidity obtainable
Favour capital safety over growth
Favour growth so the money arrives in time
quiz.explanation: The same family can hold three different risk appetites for three different pots of money: the emergency fund needs liquidity, the 3-year house fund needs capital safety, and the 25-year retirement fund can carry more risk. It is the time horizon that decides, not the age of the owner. Three years is far too short to wait out a drawdown, and maximum liquidity matters more for money you might need tomorrow.

quiz.question: What is the point of rebalancing a portfolio?
options: Shifting gradually into safer assets over time
Selling the weak assets and keeping the good ones
Raising the expected return of the whole portfolio
Holding the risk level you chose at the outset
quiz.explanation: Without rebalancing, a portfolio drifts away from its original risk appetite - the assets that rose take up a larger share, so the risk level quietly climbs above what you chose. Rebalancing is not a glide path into safety, which is a separate decision tied to a horizon; it is not a judgement about which assets are good; and it typically trims expected return slightly in exchange for holding risk steady.

quiz.question: Why does a good plan not aim purely at maximising return?
options: Because it also has to cover near-term liquidity and unexpected risk
Because return maximisation applies only to institutional investors
Because the regulator caps the return an investor is allowed to earn each year
Because a high return always brings a higher tax bill along with it
quiz.explanation: A high-returning portfolio with no cash for the next six months will force a sale at exactly the wrong moment. Protection against a shock and enough liquidity are the conditions under which the long-term investment portion is left alone to run. Institutions face the same constraint, no regulator caps returns, and tax is a consequence of gains rather than a reason to avoid them.

keyTakeaways: Wealth management looks at net worth first, and only then at investing
Asset allocation matters more than picking one winning stock
Rebalancing is what keeps risk discipline in place

summary.keyIdea: Wealth management looks at net worth first, and only then at investing
summary.commonMistake: Easily overlooked: asset allocation matters more than picking one winning stock
summary.action: Rebalancing is what keeps risk discipline in place

sections.text: Wealth management is not something 'only people with a lot of money need'. It is how you organise assets, risk and goals so that money serves your life.

sections.title: The wealth management frame
sections.subtitle: Read it left to right as a process

concepts.def: Total assets minus total liabilities - the starting point of every plan.
Splitting money across cash, bonds, equities, property and so on according to the goal.
Bringing the portfolio back to its target weights as markets move.

left.label: The common mistake
left.text: Spotting one high-returning channel and pouring money into it without considering the goal, the liquidity or the time horizon.

right.label: The right approach
right.text: Split assets by goal: near-term money, protection money, growth money and long-term money.

sections.text: A concrete example: a family with a net worth of 5bn, whose goals include an emergency fund (high liquidity, 6 months of spending), a house purchase in the next 3 years (safety first), and retirement 25 years away (able to accept more risk for growth). Wealth management properly done means allocating that 5bn into three separate 'buckets' matched to the horizon and goal of each, rather than pooling it and investing all of it under a single strategy.
Splitting that 5bn into three buckets, each with its own risk appetite

The family spends 30m a month, so a 6-month emergency fund is 180m - 3.6% of assets. The house deposit needs 1.5bn in 3 years, or 30%. The remaining 3.32bn, equivalent to 66.4%, is retirement money on a 20-year horizon. These three buckets cannot share one equity weighting, because what decides it is not the family's taste for risk but the date the money has to be there.

sections.title: One family, three different risk levels
sections.subtitle: The time horizon decides, not the personality

concepts.def: The only criterion is being able to withdraw immediately without losing value. Short-term deposits or a money market fund. Putting a single dong of equity in here means accepting you might have to sell at a loss on the day you lose your job.
Three years is far too short to wait out a recovery after a fall. If the market drops 30% in year three, the house purchase is postponed - and that is a real failure, not a temporary fluctuation.

This is the only bucket long enough for volatility risk to become something you are paid for. Keeping this bucket too safe is the biggest risk of all, because 20 years of inflation erodes purchasing power more surely than any drawdown.

sections.label: Why 'what is your risk appetite out of ten' is usually a meaningless question
sections.text: The same person, on the same day, has three different answers for the three buckets above. Collapsing them into one number and applying a single allocation to the whole 5bn puts the emergency fund somewhere too risky and the retirement money somewhere too safe - wrong at both ends simultaneously. That is why asset allocation starts from a list of goals with dates attached, and not from a personality questionnaire.

lines: Managing wealth well is about making life hold fewer surprises.
It is not about chasing the prettiest return figure.

application.title: Draw your own net worth
application.message: List your assets, debts, cash, investments and upcoming goals in a simple table so you can see which part needs protecting first.
application.secondary: Usually liquidity and a safety buffer matter more than maximising return.

practicePrompt.question: What is the core objective of the wealth management industry for individual clients?
options: Capital preservation, sustainable growth, optimal asset allocation
Advising the client to bet their whole net worth on 1 stock to trade
Promising a fixed 50%/year return with no risk attached
Selling insurance products at any cost
practicePrompt.explanation: Wealth management focuses on managing the whole financial picture: retirement planning, diversified asset allocation (equities, bonds, property) and protecting wealth across generations.
